entries.answer: What asks for a thing, an idea or a description, and it is also the general opener of any question wanting information rather than a specific time or place. The grammatical limit is that it cannot be the subject on its own, so what happened works but what did happen does not. The substitution test settles it: if the whole question can be replaced by the single word thing, it was a what-question.

entries.answer: Who asks about a person rather than a thing, and in English it divides into who and whom according to the job it does inside the sentence. Who wrote this uses it as subject and takes the verb, while to whom you gave it takes the object form after a preposition. In ordinary speech whom gets dropped, which is why it sounds formal, but it is still the form the grammar asks for.

entries.answer: Where asks about a place, and it divides the same way who does, giving where in ordinary use and whence in older ones. The usual confusion is with what, since where were you and what were you doing begin from the same verb. Where names a location and expects somewhere as an answer, while what asks for a description of an action and expects a phrase back.

patterns: when does it mean in which situation
entries.answer: When asks about a time or a point in a sequence, and it is considerably broader than a clock reading. It can mean what time is it, which day, or at what stage in a process, and the answer changes completely between those. English also allows where in the sense of in which situation, as in where I come from everything is a lesson, which is an older usage that survives mainly in fixed phrases.

entries.answer: Why asks for a reason and expects one, which is the single fact that separates it from every other question word. Because carries the same idea inside an answer, so why did you leave and because I was bored are two halves of one exchange. The awkward position is the indirect one, since why behaves as a word rather than a preposition, so the reason why has to be followed by a clause and not by a noun.

entries.answer: How asks about manner, and it is the word most often stacked with others, giving how long, how far, how often, how much and how come. How come is a genuine fixed phrase for why, and it is worth knowing whole, because learners parse it as a question about manner and it is not. Used alone it means in what way, and the answer expected is a method rather than a length or a frequency.

entries.answer: Which asks you to choose from a set that is already understood, and that is exactly what separates it from what. What is open, while which implies the options have already been mentioned, so which do you want only makes sense after somebody offered a list. The same closed and open split runs through who and whose, where a closed one needs a known set and an open one does not.
